{"id": "90:10/q06", "question": "What are the two najds in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the paired heights name moral alternatives, an infant's bodily provision, ultimate outcomes, governance, or a rhyme-driven singular path; 76:3, the blessing sequence, the dual form, and reports are cited.", "positions": [{"id": "90:10/q06/p1", "position": "They are the two moral routes of good and evil, also described as guidance and error, truth and falsehood, obedience and disobedience.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAlī, Mujāhid and many others transmit this; al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ call it the majority account. Al-Rāghib extends the pair to truth/falsehood in belief, truth/lies in speech, and good/bad deeds. Al-Nasafī says the routes lead to Paradise and Hell. Reports via al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, Anas, Abū Hurayra and Abū Umāma attribute to the Prophet a warning against preferring evil; Biqāʿī adds that sufficient little is better than distracting abundance. Ibn Kathīr says the Anas version runs uniquely through Sinān b. Saʿd, trusted by Ibn Maʿīn but criticized by Aḥmad, al-Nasāʾī and al-Jūzajānī; the al-Ḥasan and comparable reports are mursal. Al-Ḥākim authenticates Ibn Masʿūd's report, and al-Ṭabarānī transmits an Abū Umāma version. Al-Ṭabarī prefers moral paths because 76:2–3 presents showing the path as a divine favor; Ibn Jarīr, al-Qaffāl, Elmalılı and Corpus Coranicum likewise prefer this view, the latter invoking the binary dual and 91:8. ʿAlī and al-Rabīʿ b. Khuthaym reject the breast interpretation."}, {"id": "90:10/q06/p2", "position": "They are a mother's two breasts, the elevated routes through which an infant receives milk, life and nourishment.", "reasons": "Reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and, in different sources, ʿIkrima, ʿAlī, Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ b. Khuthaym and Abū Ḥāzim. The infant is guided to suckle immediately; al-Ālūsī says the breasts rise above the abdomen like two hills and cites an oath by a mother and her breasts. Elmalılı notes that the sequence of bodily gifts may motivate this reading, but rejects it because nursing is a general early-life provision rather than the human moral duty in context. Al-Wāḥidī calls it unlikely and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ strained and weak."}, {"id": "90:10/q06/p3", "position": "They are the paths of misery and happiness.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and Ibn al-Jawzī attribute this distinct formulation to Mujāhid."}, {"id": "90:10/q06/p4", "position": "They could be Paradise and Hell themselves, conceived as elevated destinations.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī proposes this from the high-road derivation, because Paradise and Fire rise above the earth."}, {"id": "90:10/q06/p5", "position": "The two heights can be understood as governance or administration.", "reasons": "Al-Tustarī records this as another interpretation beside good and evil, with a mention of 76:3."}, {"id": "90:10/q06/p6", "position": "The dual is imposed by rhyme and refers only to the virtuous path.", "reasons": "Ahrens proposes this; Corpus Coranicum finds the literal dual of good and evil more convincing in light of 76:3 and 91:8."}]}
{"id": "90:10/q07", "question": "Why are both ways called elevated paths?", "turns_on": "Whether elevation chiefly marks visibility, the effort involved in either route, or a figurative naming of evil alongside good.", "positions": [{"id": "90:10/q07/p1", "position": "Their clarity makes both routes as visible to reason as high roads are to sight.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, Ibn al-Shaykh through Bursawī and Corpus Coranicum emphasize conspicuousness; Corpus Coranicum says height recedes behind clarity and najd is broader than the next verse's ʿaqaba. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes the otherwise unique Qurʾānic word stresses visibility."}, {"id": "90:10/q07/p2", "position": "Both routes require effort; good ascends through hardship and evil entails hardship or hard consequences.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says avoiding evil itself can bring elevation and honor. Biqāʿī says either choice raises humans above animals, requires climbing, and can be made easy or difficult by divine aid; good is ringed with hardship though appealing in name, and evil can attract desire despite its difficulty. Elmalılı says action on either route requires movement, courage, patience and endurance against the body's preference for rest; one ends in safety and the other ruin. Ibn ʿĀshūr links the good route's difficulty and evil's consequences with the next verse's steep pass. Al-Sāmarrāʾī connects the word with human toil and the hard obstacle, comparing 76:3, 80:20, 1:6 and 5:16."}, {"id": "90:10/q07/p3", "position": "Good is truly elevated; evil is called elevated by predominance, imagined ascent, or a conventional pairing.", "reasons": "Bursawī and al-Ālūsī say evil actually descends from innate purity toward misery; imagination can nevertheless conceive ascent toward any goal. Elmalılı calls evil a low abyss and explains the paired name by good's predominance. Al-Ṭabrisī cites Arab paired-name usage such as al-qamarān for sun and moon, with al-Farazdaq's poetry as evidence."}]}
{"id": "90:10/q08", "question": "What sounds and recitation rules are noted at al-najdayn?", "turns_on": "Whether qalqala requires an actual pause and how neighboring sound categories are defined; no variant text is given.", "positions": [{"id": "90:10/q08/p1", "position": "The jīm of al-najdayn has medial qalqala, a forceful audible release of a still consonant.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī cites Shurayḥ and al-Mubarrad for the medial jīm; final qalqala at a pause is clearer. Al-Khalīl defines qalqala and laqlaqa as forceful sound. Ibn al-Jazarī rejects restricting qalqala to a pause: earlier waqf meant sukūn, and qalqala is neither a vowel nor a movement."}, {"id": "90:10/q08/p2", "position": "The adjacent technical discussion gives different rankings and derivations of long vowels, as well as consonant sound classes.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reports the majority's ranking of alif as strongest for madd against Ibn al-Faḥḥām's wāw, yāʾ, alif order; the majority derive fatḥa, ḍamma and kasra from alif, wāw and yāʾ. Authorities disagree whether letters precede vowels, vowels precede letters, or neither derives from the other, with some favoring the third. He defines hidden letters as hāʾ and three madd letters, the two līn letters as sākin wāw/yāʾ after fatḥ, inḥirāf as lām and rāʾ against the Basran lām-only account, and ghunna as nūn and mīm connected to the nasal cavity. These are nearby phonetic observations, with no separate variant reading of the verse stated."}]}
{"id": "90:10/q09", "question": "What does the verse imply about human moral capacity and divine agency?", "turns_on": "How acquired human choice, innate disposition, divine creation of acts, and accountability without messengers fit together.", "positions": [{"id": "90:10/q09/p1", "position": "Humans can recognize and pursue either path and are answerable for their choices, while God creates their acts and gives aid.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī distinguishes acquired capacity from autonomous independence, cites 37:96 and 76:3, and says divine guidance makes humans accountable. Quṭb calls dual capacity a wise feature of creation. Elmalılı says people begin helpless, then must thank God by choosing good and avoiding harm to self and others according to ability. Iṣlāḥī says wrongdoing can result from emotions overpowering existing knowledge."}, {"id": "90:10/q09/p2", "position": "Evil is not an inborn preference or fixed essence; secondary causes and training shape which capacity develops.", "reasons": "Elmalılı rejects the poet's claim that injustice is innate and virtue accidental. The prophetic warning that evil should not be dearer than good supports equal receptivity. He attributes Adam's lapse to Satanic seduction, and the evil-commanding soul to ignorance, corrupt upbringing or habit; training can refine or corrupt character. Natural love of received benefit differs from loving good for its own sake, and material laziness can deter both good and evil action."}, {"id": "90:10/q09/p3", "position": "Reason's guidance toward God's unity can ground accountability for shirk or atheism even without a messenger, under one contested theological view.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr states this implication of reflection on existence and oneness while noting disagreement between Ashʿarites and Māturīdīs/Muʿtazilites; he does not resolve the dispute here."}]}
{"id": "90:10/q10", "question": "How does this gift answer the surrounding human boasts?", "turns_on": "Which aspect of the passage is emphasized: the reply to arrogance, the gifts preparing responsibility, or its literary arrangement.", "positions": [{"id": "90:10/q10/p1", "position": "The created faculties and guidance show God's power and knowledge, refuting the arrogant person's claim to escape judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī points to the boast in 90:5–7 and al-Ḥasan's question about who can reckon with someone who squandered wealth: the creator of eyes, tongue, rational heart and articulate speech can destroy what He made and knows secrets. Evident favors leave no excuse for disbelief or wealth spent taunting God and His supporters. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says the God who taught the paths is still more deserving of knowledge. Jishumī says the bodily marvels make unbelief the person's own doing."}, {"id": "90:10/q10/p2", "position": "The gift sequence equips a person with perception, speech and moral direction for responsibility, which the following steep path tests.", "reasons": "Muqātil lists eyes, tongue, lips and the two moral paths. Ibn ʿĀshūr says senses acquire knowledge, speech communicates it and guidance tests action. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ calls the responsibility a difficult trust. Corpus Coranicum says the second triplet's rhyme shift underlines contrast with self-importance, while 90:11–16 judges failure to take the steep path. Al-Sāmarrāʾī connects

{"id": "90:10/q11", "question": "Which other verses clarify the two paths?", "turns_on": "Whether the comparison emphasizes the guided way in 76:3 or the moral pair in 91:7–10.", "positions": [{"id": "90:10/q11/p1", "position": "Qurʾān 76:2–3 parallels this verse by describing created, tested humans shown a way on which they may be grateful or ungrateful.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī invokes 76:2–3 to prefer the moral-path interpretation; al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ālūsī, Elmalılı, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and Corpus Coranicum likewise cite the passage. Ibn Kathīr emphasizes the shared gifts of hearing and sight. Al-Sāmarrāʾī also contrasts other Qurʾānic path words in 80:20, 1:6 and 5:16."}, {"id": "90:10/q11/p2", "position": "Qurʾān 91:7–10 spells out the pair as inspiration of wickedness and piety, followed by purification or corruption.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says the passage explains al-Balad's two routes and the command to good and prohibition of evil. Quṭb uses both passages for an account of the psyche; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, Corpus Coranicum and Iṣlāḥī make the same moral pairing."}]}
{"id": "90:10/q12", "question": "What sūra virtue report accompanies this material?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:10/q12/p1", "position": "A report promises safety from God's anger on Resurrection Day to one who recites Sūrat al-Balad.", "reasons": "Jishumī transmits it through Ubayy b. Kaʿb as a report from the Prophet; the note gives no grading."}]}
{"id": "90:10/q13", "question": "Does the extract from al-Rāzī's full text add a gloss on this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:10/q13/p1", "position": "This particular extract quotes the verses about eyes, tongue, lips and the two paths without commentary.", "reasons": "The separate al-Rāzī notes and following extract do give explanation, but this segment itself contains only verse text."}]}
{"id": "90:10/q14", "question": "What inward paths are discerned in the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:10/q14/p1", "position": "The spirit and heart each have a path, overcome respectively by ego and passion.", "reasons": "Bursawī gives this as an inward reading."}]}
{"id": "90:10/q15", "question": "What response does God's guidance invite?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:10/q15/p1", "position": "It calls for gratitude for the means God provided to live rightly.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the verse embeds this gratitude in the account of guidance and the ability to live well."}]}
{"id": "91:7/q01", "question": "How does the wāw put the soul into the oath?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:7/q01/p1", "position": "It is an oath particle governing the genitive soul and the other sworn objects.", "reasons": "Jishumī lists bāʾ, its derivative wāw, and tāʾ restricted to God's name. Kashshāf explains that the first wāw substitutes for the omitted oath verb, while coordinated wāws inherit its capacity to govern; Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿĀshūr call the nouns genitive oath objects."}]}
{"id": "91:7/q02", "question": "Whose soul, or what kind of soul, is meant by the indefinite nafs?", "turns_on": "The indefinite noun can denote a particular magnified soul or a genus; the following inspiration, purification and corruption are used to test the scope.", "positions": [{"id": "91:7/q02/p1", "position": "Human souls generally, each human self or person.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports every soul; ʿAṭāʾ and Baghawī extend it to created jinn and humans. Kashshāf, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Bursawī and Ālūsī say indefiniteness can signal multitude, citing 81:14 (Nasafī cites 69:2). Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān read a generic human genus, confirmed by inspiration and purification; Abū Ḥayyān, Ālūsī, Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Elmalılı prefer this over Adam because the sequel addresses all souls. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes it as a species including every self (82:5); Corpus Coranicum compares 75:2. Burhān explains an affirmative indefinite singular can generalize, with kull making it explicit. Rāzī notes distinct animal kinds and unknowable traits, citing 16:8, while Elmalılı restricts the morally inspired rational soul to humans."}, {"id": "91:7/q02/p2", "position": "Adam's particular soul.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan is named by Māwardī and later compilers. Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Bursawī and Ālūsī say indefiniteness magnifies him. Ālūsī calls the later change of reference istiḫdām; Abū Ḥayyān finds Adam unlikely because subsequent descriptions suit a generic soul. Elmalılı says this reading needs a special pronoun relation."}, {"id": "91:7/q02/p3", "position": "A unique sacred prophetic soul, especially the chief prophet, or the prophetic kind.", "reasons": "Rāzī argues by a hierarchy: composites are led by animals, animals by humans, humans by prophets, and prophets by one supreme leader. Elmalılı lists Muhammad, Adam, prophets collectively, and the rational human kind as magnified readings; specific prophetic readings require a special pronoun relation in the response."}, {"id": "91:7/q02/p4", "position": "The whole human composite, comprising body and spirit or personality.", "reasons": "Rāzī considers nafs as body, and Elmalılı as the spirit-body entity; Asad identifies the whole person, physical body together with elusive life essence. Qāshānī includes the composite among several possible souls."}, {"id": "91:7/q02/p5", "position": "The spirit or rational faculty governing the body.", "reasons": "Rāzī distinguishes this from body; Elmalılı likewise allows the governing spirit. Qāshānī distinguishes rational soul and animal potency impressed in animal spirit."}, {"id": "91:7/q02/p6", "position": "The indefinite marks the soul's grandeur, distinctive significance, or remarkable abilities.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows an honorific or distinctive sense. Islāḥī prefers magnitude over multitude or scarcity, citing 85:3 and 90:3. Ālūsī and Bursawī also allow grandeur without limiting the referent."}]}
{"id": "91:7/q03", "question": "What does mā in wa-mā sawwāhā denote?", "turns_on": "Whether mā is relative or infinitival, and whether the following fa-alhamahā needs an expressed divine agent.", "positions": [{"id": "91:7/q03/p1", "position": "A relative pronoun denoting God, the One who fashioned the soul.", "reasons": "Akhfash says God swears by Himself; Ṭabarī substitutes man. Abū ʿUbayda similarly uses man in the three clauses, citing 92:3 and 91:6. Ibn Qutayba says mā and man share an origin but normally divide nonhumans and humans; Abū ʿAmr and Meccan thunder speech show mā can be relative as 'that which.' Kashshāf, Nasafī, Bayḍāwī and Elmalılı favor the relative because an infinitive leaves the next verb's subject implicit or disrupts its sequence. Abū Ḥayyān cites al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Abū ʿUbayda and Ṭabarī and says mā can cover rational and nonrational beings. Jishumī reports an oath by each created object and its Maker; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the Shaper has power, knowledge and wisdom."}, {"id": "91:7/q03/p2", "position": "An infinitive or verbal noun: the soul's fashioning is sworn by.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī offers this alternative; al-Farrāʾ, Qatāda, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjāj are named by Ālūsī and Elmalılı. Naḥḥās says mā, rather than man, fits the fashioning itself. Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār wants the Creator's oath to follow oaths by created things; Study Quran reports an attribution to Qurṭubī preferring nominal phrases. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the clauses effects of divine power; Islāḥī sees workmanship and accountability. Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī and Nasafī object that the next fa-alhamahā lacks an expressed agent or coordinated structure. Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī reply that God is understood from context and verb-noun coordination is possible; Ālūsī adds that temporal order may be customary and that the objection burdens both parses. Elmalılı concedes coordination but prefers an expressed Maker."}, {"id": "91:7/q03/p3", "position": "Mā refers to the wise cosmic order or purposes behind the acts.", "reasons": "Ālūsī records the proposal that building, spreading, shaping and inspiration are metaphorically predicated of this order, but dismisses it as far-fetched."}, {"id": "91:7/q03/p4", "position": "Mā means what each feminine object built or formed.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum appeals to feminine -hā agreeing with sky, earth and soul, and distinguishes the construction from 92:3, where mā may refer to what God created."}]}
{"id": "91:7/q04", "question": "Why use mā rather than man for the Shaper?", "turns_on": "The sources dispute whether mā can point to God and whether it adds a descriptive or enigmatic effect.", "positions": [{"id": "91:7/q04/p1", "position": "It evokes the Maker's power and wisdom, or suspense and wonder.", "reasons": "Kashshāf and Nasafī say mā supplies a descriptive force, as in mighty builder and wise shaper; Abū Ḥayyān objects that neither mā nor man can function as a descriptive adjective. Elmalılı says the ambiguity provokes wonder and introduces an unknown God by His works; Corpus Coranicum says the enigmatic Creator is explicitly named at 91:14."}, {"id": "91:7/q04/p2", "position": "The ordinary distribution favors man for a person and mā for a thing or act.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba gives this human/nonhuman distribution; Naḥḥās says referring to God as 'the One who proportioned' would require man; the grammarians reported by Elmalılı prefer the infinitive to avoid mā referring to God."}]}

{"id": "91:7/q06", "question": "What does the suffix -hā in sawwāhā refer back to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:7/q06/p1", "position": "It refers to the feminine soul, as the parallel suffixes refer to sky and earth.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says feminine agreement excludes referring the suffix to mā."}]}
{"id": "91:7/q07", "question": "What does fashioning or proportioning the soul consist of?", "turns_on": "Whether taswiyah describes bodily symmetry, the rational faculty, preparation for perfection, or a moral-spiritual balance.", "positions": [{"id": "91:7/q07/p1", "position": "Forming and evenly proportioning its body, limbs, senses and outward organs.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī, Mujāhid, Ibn ʿAbbās and others gloss creation and its balanced limbs. Jishumī adds senses and channels; Rāzī appeals to anatomy; Biqāʿī includes substances, accidents and contrary humors. Ibn ʿĀshūr says without disparity, compares 82:7 and links taswiyah to precise making in 75:38 and 87:2. Corpus Coranicum notes 75:38, 87:2 and 82:7. Ibn al-Jawzī refers back to 82:7."}, {"id": "91:7/q07/p2", "position": "Perfecting intellect, discernment and inward faculties.", "reasons": "Māwardī says reason distinguishes humans from animals; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say completed intellect and reflection prepare inspiration. Rāzī names hearing, sight, imagination, thought and memory. Ālūsī and Kur'an Yolu include spiritual powers, their functions and organs. Qāshānī describes readiness for perfection between bodily and spiritual worlds."}, {"id": "91:7/q07/p3", "position": "Preparing the soul or body for its intended perfection and the breathing of spirit.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī glosses sawwā as preparing. Bursawī says creation endowed readiness for perfection. Elmalılı distinguishes bodily preparation for spirit (15:29; 38:72) from ordering outward and inward powers; Asad calls it forming by an intended pattern (87:2). Islāḥī treats taswiyah as the final stage of creation (87:2)."}, {"id": "91:7/q07/p4", "position": "Creating the soul upright upon a sound natural disposition.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr invokes 30:30, the Prophet's report that newborns have fitra before parents turn them toward other religions (Bukhārī and Muslim), and ʿIyāḍ's report that God made servants upright monotheists before devils diverted them."}, {"id": "91:7/q07/p5", "position": "Making souls equal in health and equal in punishment.", "reasons": "Māwardī attributes this detail, within the universal-soul view, to Ibn Jurayj."}, {"id": "91:7/q07/p6", "position": "Balancing the animal, composite or rational soul between bodily lowliness and spiritual elevation.", "reasons": "Qāshānī likens the balance to neither east nor west (24:35), a proportioned temperament, or readiness for perfection between two worlds, depending on the soul meant."}]}
{"id": "91:7/q08", "question": "How is fashioning linked by the following fāʾ to inspiration?", "turns_on": "Whether fāʾ demands immediate temporal succession, and whether inspiration can share the syntax of the oath clause.", "positions": [{"id": "91:7/q08/p1", "position": "Fashioning makes intellect ready, then God inspires the soul.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim connects the fāʾ to the shaping clause; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say completed intellect and reflection explain the subsequent inspiration. Ālūsī says adjusted organs and thought are accompanied by guidance along two paths (90:10), which grows with the faculties."}, {"id": "91:7/q08/p2", "position": "The sequence is problematic if inspiration is taken as immediately after bodily formation.", "reasons": "The reported objection says formation comes before breathing the soul, while inspiration comes after maturity. Ālūsī replies that guidance begins with the soul's formation and develops with it; elsewhere he says the fāʾ may express customary rather than literal temporal order. Ṭībī appeals to balanced cadence against verb coordination, which Ālūsī says assumes an independent following clause."}]}
{"id": "91:7/q09", "question": "What does the fashioned soul's nature teach about moral choice and accountability?", "turns_on": "The notes set human capacity and choice beside reports that deeds and destinations are divinely decreed.", "positions": [{"id": "91:7/q09/p1", "position": "It is equipped to discern and choose good or evil, so purification brings success and corruption loss.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says even the ignorant recognize righteous and wicked deeds. Quṭb traces equal readiness to earthly clay and breathed spirit. Biqāʿī says capacity and choice attend differing dispositions; Ibn al-Zubayr calls the capacity acquired, not independent, citing 90:10, 76:3 and 37:96. Islāḥī calls the soul a witness to its Maker and accountability, comparing closing one's eyes while walking; divine favors should be used gratefully. Kur'an Yolu says human superiority entails moral powers. Corpus Coranicum reads verse 8's opposed capacities and verses 9–10's outcomes as the oath's moral movement."}, {"id": "91:7/q09/p2", "position": "God decreed and prepared each person's deeds and final destination.", "reasons": "The Prophet, in Ibn Abī Ḥātim's report, says deeds are decreed yet people act because each is prepared for the created destination. Thaʿlabī's Abū al-Aswad answers ʿImrān that all is decreed and God owns creation (21:23); another Thaʿlabī note says God prepares the two destinations. Ālūsī transmits the two Muzayna men's question and the Prophet's answer citing 91:7–8, with Bukhārī, Muslim and Abū Dāwūd named."}]}
{"id": "91:7/q10", "question": "What is the oath's answer or implied conclusion?", "turns_on": "Whether the complement is read as the explicit purification contrast or as a broader implicit warning.", "positions": [{"id": "91:7/q10/p1", "position": "The answer is that whoever purifies the soul succeeds, while whoever corrupts it fails.", "reasons": "Akhfash identifies qad aflaḥa man zakkāhā. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the oath prepares this contrast; Islāḥī says the soul's innate moral awareness witnesses the same outcome. Corpus Coranicum reads verses 9–10 as the antithetical result of the oath series."}, {"id": "91:7/q10/p2", "position": "Its implied conclusion is God's differing dispositions and the need to purify oneself in view of resurrection.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says God prepared souls for purification or corruption through capacity and choice."}, {"id": "91:7/q10/p3", "position": "Its suppressed complement includes the threatened destruction of rebellious nations.", "reasons": "Islāḥī says ellipsis permits everything evident from the oaths; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the oath confirms the implicit destruction threat carried by the news."}]}
{"id": "91:7/q11", "question": "How does the soul oath relate to the preceding cosmic oaths and the sūra's argument?", "turns_on": "How the sequence shifts from cosmic signs to the human moral subject and the Creator.", "positions": [{"id": "91:7/q11/p1", "position": "The series moves from visible cosmic creation to the human soul and, through it, to the unseen Creator and moral duty.", "reasons": "Rāzī says heaven and earth are simple upper and lower bodies, with ensouled beings the noblest composites; sensory signs lead reason to divine majesty. Asad sees bodily, emotional and intellectual personhood following cosmic contemplation. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the series displays wise and powerful creation; Burhān lists oaths by God, His acts and created things."}, {"id": "91:7/q11/p4", "position": "This sūra continues the warning of Sūrat al-Balad to Quraysh.", "reasons": "Islāḥī says Balad warned that Mecca's prosperity came through Abraham's prayer and the House (90:4), while Shams warns what follows if Quraysh persist in arrogance."}]}

{"id": "91:8/q02", "question": "How does fa-alhamaha connect grammatically to the preceding oath?", "turns_on": "The antecedent of mā, whether it is a relative naming the Maker, a verbal noun naming the making, or a figurative cosmic order, controls the subject and coordination of alhamahā.", "positions": [{"id": "91:8/q02/p1", "position": "It is coordinated with the soul's fashioning, with fa marking inspiration as its consequence or sequence.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim links the fa to 'the soul and what fashioned it.' Al-Ālūsī says the sequence may be customary, and development of faculties makes the interval unobjectionable."}, {"id": "91:8/q02/p2", "position": "It is an independent verbal clause following the relative mā, whose subject is the divine Maker.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī objects that verbal-noun mā leaves alhamahā coordinated to a noun without a subject; Elmalılı prefers the relative construction as syntactically clearer and naming the Maker. {"id": "91:8/q08", "question": "What other rhetorical choices shape the paired wording?", "turns_on": "The notes discuss either the ellipsis between the pair or the grammatical force of the paired nouns.", "positions": [{"id": "91:8/q08/p1", "position": "The pairing uses ellipsis to make each named quality evoke its opposite.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī identifies iḥtibāk: vice implies omitted stillness or restraint, while piety implies the omitted absence of fear."}, {"id": "91:8/q08/p2", "position": "The nouns name the moral states or sinful acts as objects of inspiration.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī calls both verbal nouns functioning as direct objects; Elmalılı argues taqwā is a result noun, so fujūr names sinful acts rather than merely committing them, with prohibition and command implicit."}]}
